items.title: 47 (Critical Thinking): Deflection of currents and winds in each hemisphere

body.html: (a) A northern-hemisphere ocean current flows east across the North Atlantic. Which way is it <sub>deflected? (b) A southern-hemisphere current flows east in the South Atlantic. Which way is it deflected? (c) Which way does</sub> <sub>the South Pacific gyre circulate?</sub>

Currents are moving water in Earth's rotating frame, so they are deflected by the Coriolis "force": to the right of <sub>the direction of motion in the northern hemisphere, and to the left in the southern hemisphere.</sub>

Facing east, right is south, and left is north. In the southern hemisphere, deflection to the left in each part of the flow, <sub>together with the continents that block the flow, makes large gyres that turn counterclockwise.</sub>

answer.html: (a) South (to the right of eastward motion). (b) North (to the left of eastward motion). (c) The South Pacific gyre <sub>circulates counterclockwise.</sub>

check.html: The south-hemisphere rule is the mirror image of the north, where gyres turn clockwise.

items.title: Focus Question: Why are some vehicles more likely to roll over than others?

body.html: A vehicle is stable while its center of mass is above its base of support. To roll over, it must tilt until the center of mass passes beyond the wheels' outer edge.

A vehicle with a high center of mass needs to tilt only a small angle for the center of mass to be outside its base. A vehicle with a low center of mass has to be tilted much farther (raising its center of mass more) before it tips. A narrower wheel track also shrinks the base.

answer.html: Taller vehicles (higher center of mass) and narrower vehicles roll over more easily, because a smaller tilt moves the center of mass outside the base of support.

items.title: Get It? Describe when an object is the most stable

answer.html: An object is most stable when its center of mass is as low as possible and its base of support is as broad as possible, with the center of mass directly above the base.

items.title: Get It? Explain why Hurricanes Katia, Irma, and Jose rotate counterclockwise

answer.html: They are in the northern hemisphere. Air flowing toward each low-pressure center is deflected to its right by the Coriolis "force," so each system circulates counterclockwise (see the Encounter the Phenomenon answer).

items.title: 41: Examples of equilibrium types

body.html: Translational equilibrium: net force = 0. Rotational equilibrium: net torque = 0. An object can have one without the other.

(a) Net torque zero but net force not zero: a ball in free fall or a rock thrown through the air. Gravity acts at the center of mass, so there is no torque about it, but the net force is mg. A car speeding up along a straight road is another example (it is not spinning, but it is accelerating). (b) Net force zero but net torque not zero: a steering wheel turned by two hands pushing on opposite sides with equal and opposite tangential forces. The forces cancel, but the torques add and the wheel gains angular velocity.

answer.html: (a) A freely falling ball (rotationally balanced but accelerating). (b) A steering wheel being turned by two equal and opposite forces at opposite edges (net force zero, net torque not zero).

items.title: 42: Can the center of mass be where the object has no mass?

answer.html: Yes. The center of mass is a balance point of the mass distribution, not necessarily a place where material exists. For a ring, a hoop, a doughnut or a boomerang, the center of mass is in the empty middle.

items.title: 43: Why is a vehicle raised high on risers less stable?

body.html: Raising the body raises the center of mass while the wheel base (the base of support) stays the same. A smaller tilt is then enough to put the center of mass outside the base, and the vehicle rolls over. Also, raising the center of mass means a given sideways force produces a larger tipping torque about the wheel contact point.

answer.html: The higher center of mass reaches the tipping point with a smaller tilt, with the same base width, so the vehicle is less stable.

items.title: 44: Center of mass of a roll of masking tape

answer.html: At the geometric center of the roll, on the axis through the middle of the hole. This point is in the empty hole, which shows that the center of mass need not be on the material. By symmetry, the mass is spread evenly around the axis and across the roll's width.

items.title: 45: Find the center of mass of this textbook

question.html: Method (the book's method): Hang the book from a point near one corner by a string or pin and let it stop swinging. Draw a vertical line on the cover from the suspension point (use a plumb line as a guide). Repeat from a second point, such as an adjacent corner. The two lines cross at the center of mass (in the plane of the cover; for a uniform book it lies at the middle of the thickness too). A third suspension point should confirm the same crossing. Alternatively, balance the book on a ruler edge in two directions.

answer.html: Suspend the book from two (or three) different points, drawing the vertical line below each. The center of mass is where the lines intersect, about the geometric center of the book.

items.title: 46: Forces on a penny sliding on a turntable

body.html: In the lab (inertial) frame, a penny moving in a circle needs a net inward (centripetal) force. Only real forces count.

The real forces are the penny's weight (down), the normal force from the turntable (up), and static friction (horizontal, toward the center). Friction supplies the centripetal force 𝐹= 𝑚𝜔<sup>2</sup>𝑟. As ω increases, the required force grows, and at the highest speed it exceeds the maximum static friction, so the penny slides. No real outward force acts; the "outward push" is centrifugal "force," which appears only in the turntable's rotating frame.

answer.html: Gravity (down), the normal force (up), and static friction (toward the center). Friction is the only horizontal force; the penny slides when the needed centripetal force exceeds the maximum friction. There is no real outward force.

items.title: 47 (Critical Thinking): Direction of surface ocean currents in each hemisphere

body.html: Currents are moving water in Earth's rotating frame, so they are deflected by the Coriolis "force": to the right of the direction of motion in the northern hemisphere, and to the left in the southern hemisphere (like the winds, and like the book's projectile).

A current heading toward the equator is deflected westward, and one heading away from the equator is deflected eastward. In the northern hemisphere this deflection to the right, together with the continents that block the flow, makes large circular patterns (gyres) that turn clockwise. In the southern hemisphere the deflection is to the left, which gives counterclockwise gyres.

answer.html: Northern hemisphere: surface currents curve to the right and circulate clockwise. Southern hemisphere: currents curve to the left and circulate counterclockwise.

check.html: This is the reverse of how winds circulate around low-pressure centers (counterclockwise in the north), as expected for flow around high-pressure regions.
